name: Margin Check
question: What does each sale really leave?
scope: Up to 10 products, services or projects; one price-or-cost scenario; a one-page summary with up to three points to investigate.
problem: Three projects brought in $50,000. The owner wants to know how much is left after the costs directly needed to deliver them.

inputs.note: Delivery costs are costs assigned to these projects. Shared overheads, tax and finance costs are not included.

metrics.label: Money left after delivery costs
metrics.detail: Before overheads and tax. This is not final profit.

finding: Sales of $50,000 minus $38,000 in delivery costs leave $12,000. That is $24 of every $100 sold, before overheads and tax.
nextStep: Check that every delivery cost is included before setting the next price.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: For every $100 sold, $76 pays for delivery and $24 is left. The business still has to pay its overheads and tax.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: The three projects bring in $50,000 and cost $38,000 to deliver. Project A leaves 30% of its sales; Projects B and C leave 20%. Check prices and delivery effort to understand why.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Include all delivery costs, compare the projects that leave less, and use a realistic cost estimate for the next quote.

scenario.title: What if delivery costs rise?
scenario.description: Sales stay at $50,000, but delivery costs rise by $5,000. Money left falls to $7,000, or 14% of sales.
scenario.note: The extra cost is an example to test, not a prediction.

deliverables: A comparison of money left after delivery costs for the three projects
One cost-increase scenario
A one-page summary with up to three checks to make before the next quote
cautions: Money left after delivery costs still has to cover overheads, other costs and tax. It is not final profit.
The cost increase is an assumption, not a prediction.

name: Four-Week Cash Snapshot
question: Could cash get tight in the next four weeks?
scope: Opening cash plus up to 20 dated expected receipts and payments; a four-week forecast; one delayed-payment scenario; a one-page summary.
problem: The business starts with $30,000 in cash. Its owner wants to know whether the next four weeks of expected receipts will cover the payments due.
inputLabel: Opening cash $30,000 plus eight dated entries

inputs.note: Fictional forecast for 2–29 November 2026. Receipts and payments occur on the stated dates. No borrowing facility is assumed.

metrics.label: Cash at the end, if paid on time
Lowest cash, if paid on time
Cash gap if payment is late
metrics.detail: Cash would fall to −$10,000 on 20 November.

finding: If customers pay on time, cash ends at $35,000. If the $40,000 payment arrives ten days late, the business is $10,000 short on 20 November, even though cash still ends at $35,000.
nextStep: Confirm when the $40,000 will arrive and prepare a backup plan before the supplier bill is due.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: There is enough money overall, but a bill may come due before a customer pays. The dates matter as much as the total.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: There is $15,000 available when a $25,000 supplier bill falls due. If the $40,000 customer payment has not arrived, the gap is $10,000.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Check the customer’s payment date and which bills cannot move. Agree a backup plan, such as an agreed payment-date change or cash already set aside.

scenario.title: What if one customer pays late?
scenario.description: Only receipt C changes: 16 November becomes 26 November. All other amounts and dates stay the same.
scenario.note: A negative forecast balance represents funding needed; it does not assume the bank will permit an overdraft. The dated entries were checked as well as the weekly totals.

deliverables: A four-week cash forecast from the eight entries
One delayed-receipt scenario
A one-page summary of the potential gap and receipt/payment questions
cautions: Expected cash receipts are not the same as revenue or profit.
Unlisted payments, taxes or changes in timing would change the forecast.

name: Plan vs Actual Review
question: Where did results differ from the plan?
scope: An existing budget and matching actuals for up to three months and 15 categories; the three largest differences by value; a one-page summary.
problem: The owner had a two-month budget, but less money was left after operating costs than expected. Which differences need attention first?

inputs.note: Only sales, delivery costs, payroll and rent are included. Any other costs, interest and tax still need to be considered.

metrics.label: Planned money left after listed costs
Actual money left after listed costs

finding: There is $23,000 less left than planned: $15,000 from lower sales, $6,000 from extra payroll and $2,000 from extra delivery costs.
nextStep: Start with sales, then ask the team about staffing costs and delivery costs.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: After the costs shown, $22,000 is left instead of the planned $45,000. This compares business results; it does not show when cash is received or paid.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: Sales are lower than planned, while payroll and delivery costs are higher. The figures show where to look, but not why it happened.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Review the $15,000 sales gap first. Then check the $6,000 extra payroll and $2,000 extra delivery costs with the people responsible.

scenario.title: The three largest differences
scenario.description: Add the two months together, then compare the largest differences.
scenario.note: Lower sales and higher costs reduce the money left. Rent matches its $20,000 plan.

deliverables: A matching monthly plan-versus-actual comparison
The top three differences by value
A one-page summary with possible drivers and team questions
cautions: A difference from the plan is a question to investigate, not proof of its cause.
Only the listed costs are included. This is not final profit.
calculationNotes: Surplus change: −15,000 sales − 6,000 payroll − 2,000 direct costs = −23,000.
Eight monthly rows cover two months and four unique categories, within the starter limits.

name: AI Finance Workflow Setup
question: Can one spreadsheet become a clearer first draft?
scope: One approved spreadsheet input to one draft commentary workflow in the client’s approved ChatGPT or Claude setup; reusable prompt, input template, sample draft, basic tests, human-review checklist and walkthrough.
problem: The owner writes the same monthly explanation of sales and costs. A clear template can help produce a first draft for a person to check.
inputLabel: One approved input template, with three fictional rows

inputs.note: This sample commentary is prewritten, not a live AI chat.

metrics.label: Planned money left after listed costs
Actual money left after listed costs

finding: The draft highlights $10,000 less sales than planned. The two cost differences cancel each other out. A person must check the figures and the explanation.
nextStep: Choose an approved tool and template, test it with known numbers, and name the person who will review each draft.
draftCommentary: Sales were $90,000 against a $100,000 plan. Delivery costs were $2,000 below plan, while other operating costs were $2,000 above plan. After the costs shown, $5,000 was left instead of the planned $15,000. Check what changed in sales; these figures alone do not explain the reason.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: One spreadsheet can become a first draft of a business update. This sample is prewritten, not a live AI chat.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: A consistent template makes the task easier to repeat. It does not guarantee a correct answer. Here, lower sales explain the $10,000 gap after the two cost differences cancel out.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Use approved data and tools. Test the draft with known figures, then have a person check it before sharing or using it.

scenario.title: Basic checks before a draft is used
scenario.description: Simple checks to try before using a draft for real work.

rows.expected: Check the result is $5,000 actual and $15,000 planned money left after listed costs.

rows.test: A required actual amount is blank
rows.expected: Stop and ask for the missing figure; do not treat a blank as zero.
Flag the invalid value; do not produce numerical conclusions.

rows.test: A note claims a reason without supporting data
rows.expected: Label it unverified or ask for evidence; do not present it as fact.

deliverables: A reusable prompt and one input template
A sample draft and simple checks to test it
A human-review checklist and walkthrough
cautions: All AI outputs require human review before financial decisions.
Tool subscriptions, API usage, custom integrations and ongoing support are separate.
Excel add-in setup depends on compatibility and administrator approval.
Use only tools and data approved for the intended purpose. This demonstration uses fictional data.
calculationNotes: Surplus change: −10,000 sales + 2,000 direct-cost saving − 2,000 other-cost increase = −10,000.
The draft is stored text. No model call is made by these example files.

name: Plan a hire or expansion
question: What would a new hire need to pay for itself?
scope: Illustrative tailored planning work. The actual budget, forecast, scenarios, deliverables, timeline and fee are agreed separately after discussing the decision.
problem: The owner is considering a hire costing $30,000 per month plus $20,000 of one-time setup cash. Would the expected extra sales cover the ongoing cost?

inputs.note: Start with $60,000 cash. Half of sales is left after delivery costs. All sales are collected and monthly costs paid in the same month. The hire cost includes the employment costs assumed here. Setup payments are shown separately.

metrics.label: Cash at first month-end, expected case

finding: If $50 of each extra $100 in sales is left after delivery costs, the business needs $60,000 more sales each month to cover a $30,000 hire. The one-time setup also uses $20,000 of cash.
nextStep: Check how quickly those extra sales could arrive, the full cost of the hire and how much cash to keep available.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: In the expected case, the hire brings $60,000 more sales. Half is left after delivery costs, which just covers the $30,000 hire. The monthly amount left after listed costs stays at $30,000.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: Each extra $100 in sales leaves $50 after delivery costs. Covering a $30,000 hire therefore needs $60,000 of extra sales. With only $20,000 extra sales, just $10,000 is left after the listed monthly costs.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Check whether the extra sales are realistic and how long they may take. Include payment delays and any costs missing from this example.

scenario.title: What changes in the first month?
scenario.description: Opening cash is $60,000 in every case; one-time setup cash is deducted only in the hire cases.
scenario.note: The monthly amount left excludes the one-time setup payment, unlisted costs, interest and tax. Payment delays or different delivery costs would change the result.

deliverables: An agreed budget or scenario model around the hiring decision
A comparison of recurring costs, one-time cash needs and assumptions
A walkthrough of the trade-offs and information still needed
cautions: Expected sales are assumptions, not guaranteed results.
This is a small illustration of tailored work, not a fixed-price starter package.
Scope, deliverables, timeline and fees are agreed separately.
calculationNotes: No hire left after listed costs: 200,000 − 100,000 − 70,000 = 30,000.
Expected hire left after listed costs: 260,000 − 130,000 − 70,000 − 30,000 = 30,000.
Lower-sales hire left after listed costs: 220,000 − 110,000 − 70,000 − 30,000 = 10,000.
Expected closing cash: 60,000 + 30,000 − 20,000 = 70,000; lower-sales closing cash = 50,000.

name: Understand cash and profit
question: Why can profit look positive while cash falls?
scope: Illustrative deeper review of pricing, margins or cash flow. The area to investigate, deliverables, timeline and fee are agreed separately.
problem: The accounts show $30,000 profit before unlisted costs and tax, yet cash falls by $15,000. Why?

rows.item: Additional unsold stock bought and paid for

inputs.note: No opening customer or supplier balances are involved. The additional unsold stock is separate from the cost of items sold. No other cash movements, depreciation, interest or tax are included.

metrics.label: Profit before unlisted costs and tax

finding: Customers still owe $40,000, and $20,000 went into extra stock. The business has also not yet paid $15,000 of supplier bills. Together, these explain why cash fell by $15,000 despite the $30,000 profit shown.
nextStep: Review the unpaid customer invoices and unsold stock, while making sure the outstanding supplier payments stay in the cash plan.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: A sale can count in the accounts before the customer pays. A stock purchase can use cash before the stock is sold. That is why profit and cash can move differently.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: Customers still owe $40,000, extra stock used $20,000, and $15,000 of supplier bills remain unpaid. Those three differences explain the cash change.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Confirm when customers will pay, check whether the extra stock is needed, and keep unpaid supplier bills in the cash plan.

scenario.title: From profit shown to cash change
scenario.description: Start with the profit shown, then adjust for money not yet received or paid and the extra stock purchase.

rows.item: Profit before unlisted costs and tax
Add supplier costs not yet paid
Less extra unsold stock paid for

scenario.note: Closing cash is opening cash $50,000 plus the $15,000 net outflow: $35,000. Unpaid supplier bills are still obligations.

deliverables: An agreed review of the relevant profit and cash drivers
A clear reconciliation or model using the agreed data
A walkthrough of the findings and next questions
cautions: The profit shown excludes unlisted costs, depreciation, interest and tax. It is not final profit.
The example is deliberately simplified; a real reconciliation may have additional adjustments.
Tailored scope, deliverables, timeline and fees are agreed separately.

name: Assess marketing performance
question: Are cheaper new customers actually more profitable?
scope: Analysis of existing marketing spend, sales and customer-profitability data, with assumptions and gaps made clear. Tailored scope and fee are agreed separately.
problem: Social ads bring in new customers more cheaply. But do their first purchases leave enough to cover delivery and advertising?
inputLabel: Two fictional channels, one first-order cohort

inputs.note: Assume 60 distinct new paying customers, each assigned once to a channel using the supplied records. Revenue is after discounts and refunds; direct costs include fulfilment. Repeat purchases, shared overheads, interest and tax are excluded.

metrics.label: Search: left after delivery and ads
Social: left after delivery and ads
Search: ad cost per new customer
Social: ad cost per new customer

finding: Search leaves $6,000 after delivery and ads. Social’s first purchases fall $800 short of covering those costs, despite the lower cost of finding a customer.
nextStep: Check which ads customers came from, refunds and repeat purchases before changing the budget.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: After delivery and ad costs, Search leaves $6,000 and Social is $800 short. This only covers first purchases, before overheads and tax.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: Each Search customer leaves $800 after delivery, then costs $500 in ads. Each Social customer leaves $180, but costs $200 in ads. Order size, discounts or the items bought may explain the difference; check the records.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Count each customer once, include refunds and all costs, and check which channel each sale came from. Then look at repeat purchases before deciding what to change.

scenario.title: Follow the money per customer
scenario.description: Divide each channel’s sales, delivery costs and ad spend by its number of new paying customers.
scenario.note: Matching sales to a channel does not prove the ads caused those sales.

deliverables: A performance analysis using existing spend, sales and cost records
Clearly defined measures, assumptions and evidence gaps
Questions and options to review before taking action
cautions: This service covers performance analysis, not campaign management, SEO or content production.
Only first purchases are included, before overheads and tax. Future repeat purchases are excluded.
Tailored scope, deliverables, timeline and fees are agreed separately.
calculationNotes: Search ad cost per new customer: 10,000 ÷ 20 = 500; Social: 8,000 ÷ 40 = 200.
Search money left per customer after ads: 6,000 ÷ 20 = 300; Social: −800 ÷ 40 = −20.

name: Make reporting more useful
question: Which numbers should lead to a useful conversation?
scope: An agreed reporting pack, performance dashboard or defined spreadsheet workflow, with documentation and a team handover. Tailored scope and fee are agreed separately.
problem: The owner sees sales rising, but the monthly report does not make the next decisions clear. A short view should connect important numbers to questions and owners.
inputLabel: Four inputs from two fictional monthly reports

rows.item: Overdue customer invoices at month end

inputs.note: Both months use the same definitions. Overdue payments and cash are measured at month-end. The example’s warning levels are chosen for this business, not industry rules.

metrics.label: Share left after delivery costs
metrics.detail: $35 left from every $100 sold, down from $40. Before overheads and tax.

finding: Sales rose 20%. Money left after delivery costs rose only 5%, from $40,000 to $42,000. That means the share left fell from 40% to 35%. The amount customers owe past its due date rose from $10,000 to $25,000.
nextStep: Ask sales or operations why less is left from each dollar of sales. Ask finance when the overdue money should arrive.

qa.question: What does this mean?
qa.answer: Rising sales are not the whole story. A smaller share is left after delivery costs, and more money is overdue from customers.

qa.question: Why is this happening?
qa.answer: Delivery costs rose 30% while sales rose 20%. Check prices, the types of work sold and delivery costs to understand why. The figures do not explain why customer payments are late.

qa.question: What should I do next?
qa.answer: Agree what each number means, who checks it and when it needs attention. Keep a simple update and checking process.

scenario.title: Turn each warning sign into a question
scenario.description: These example warning levels are chosen for the fictional business.

rows.question: What changed in prices, sales mix or direct costs?
Which invoices are overdue, and when is collection expected?
Above this example threshold; still check upcoming payments.

scenario.note: A warning level tells someone to check. It does not prove that the business or its cash is safe.

deliverables: An agreed reporting pack, dashboard or spreadsheet workflow
Definitions, update instructions and validation checks
A handover so the team can own the reporting process
cautions: Money left after delivery costs still has to cover overheads and tax. It is not final profit.
This is a sample report, not a live connection to business records.
Tailored scope, deliverables, timeline and fees are agreed separately.
